about: Noviomagus (Nijmegen), the king's house on the Waal: one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/noviomagus.md and the spine. A draft for the user to overwrite.

ports.summary: Noviomagus is a king's house, not a town: a palace being built inside the walls of an old Roman fort, on a hill above the south bank of the Waal, with a small settlement of boatmen, craftsmen and farmers on the bank below. In 793 the king is elsewhere and the place is half a building yard and half a farm that feeds a court which has not come. A merchant comes for what a court eats and wears when it does come, for the ear of the men who serve it, and because every count on the lower Rhine must one day stand in that hall.
ports.seasons: The year here is the court's: when the king keeps Lent and Easter at the palace, a few hundred mouths arrive by ship and everything is wanted at once; in spring and autumn he hunts the Ketil wood, and the assemblies fall in May, June and October. Between courts the bank is quiet, the river runs high after the thaw and low at harvest, and the cellarer buys ahead.

history.text: About this year the Romans built the ditched fort on the hilltop whose walls still partly stand in 793, and the thick, high wall of tuff along the river bank.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts; mijngelderland.nl, Rijke Merovingen; noviomagus.nl kalendarium (dossier VP, MG, Kal)

history.text: Gold tremisses reading Niomago, found in the Escharen hoard of 590-600, were very likely struck here. No mint is known in the game's years.
history.source: verhaalvangelderland.nl, Vroege middeleeuwen: economie en uitwisseling; noviomagus.nl, Munt (dossier VvG, Munt)

history.text: About this year burial with weapons and pots ended and the old grave fields were closed: over 2,000 graves, the largest early medieval grave field found in the Netherlands.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Geschiedenis van Nijmegen; mijngelderland.nl (dossier GN, MG)

history.text: Charles kept Easter here. A charter of 8 June, dated 'in Niumago palacio publico', gave Leusden and four forests to Saint Martin's of Utrecht.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 777; nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts (dossier ARF, VP)

history.text: The palace that Charles 'began at Nimeguen, on the Waal, the stream that washes the south side of the island of the Batavians' is perhaps still unfinished; historians date its completion about 804 or later.
history.source: Einhard, Life of Charlemagne c. 17, tr. S. E. Turner 1880; nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts (dossier Ein 17, VP)

history.text: Charles came by ship down the Moselle and the Rhine and kept Lent and Easter here. The capitulary made here capped famine prices by the modius (oats 2 d, barley 3, spelt 3, rye 4, cleaned wheat 6), called buying at harvest to sell dear 'shameful gain', forbade new tolls and ordered church treasure guarded.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 806; MGH Capitularia I no. 46, Nijmegen, March 806 (dossier ARF, Cap806)

history.text: Charles kept Lent and Easter here after a mild, sickly winter. Eardwulf, the exiled king of Northumbria, came to him and went on to Rome. The capitulary of April capped a best double cloak at 20 solidi, a single at 10, a marten or otter coat at 30.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 808; capitulary of Nijmegen, April 808 (dossier ARF, Cap808)

history.text: Louis the emperor hunted here twenty days, after the wooden portico fell on him at Aachen.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 817 (dossier ARF)

history.text: In May the division of the realm among the emperor's sons was read again here and sworn. Louis came down the Maas by ship.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 821 (dossier ARF)

history.text: Louis hunted here in spring, and again in autumn with his son Lothar.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 825 (dossier ARF)

history.text: An assembly waited here for Horik, son of King Godfrid of the Danes, who had promised to come and did not.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 827 (dossier ARF)

history.text: About this year Gerward, the palace librarian, who had charge of the palace works and buildings, was here; on the road to Aachen he heard of a healing from his host, questioned the woman and told the emperor next day.
history.source: Einhard, Translatio Marcellini et Petri (dossier Trans)

history.text: About the first of October the assembly was held here so that Saxons and East Franks could come, and Louis recovered his power from his sons.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 830 (dossier AB)

history.text: Northmen took tribute on Walcheren and at Dorestad. Louis hurried here and they left at once.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 837 (dossier AB)

history.text: In May and June the coast defences were shared out here; a Danish fleet drowned in a storm; Louis the German was stripped of lands.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 838; Annales Fuldenses 838 (dossier AB, AF)

history.text: Lothar, in the fort at Noviomagus, saw Dorestad burned by the Northmen and could not avenge it.
history.source: Annales Xantenses 846 (dossier AX)

history.text: Charles the Bald met Rorik the Northman, lord of Dorestad, in the palace and bound him by treaty.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 870 (dossier AB)

history.text: A fleet of Northmen entered the Waal, put 'a very strong rampart and walls' round the palace and wintered in it. Eberhard the Saxon, son of Count Meginhard, was taken captive; his mother Evesa ransomed him 'at a great price'.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 880; Regino of Prüm 881 (dossier AF, Reg)

history.text: Louis the Younger besieged the palace in a hard winter, failed, and left on the Northmen's promise to go. They burned the palace and their works and made for the mouths of the Rhine.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 880; Regino of Prüm 881 (dossier AF, Reg)

history.text: Charles the Simple was here.
history.source: Regino of Prüm 898 (dossier Reg)

history.text: Otto the king held an assembly here.
history.source: noviomagus.nl kalendarium (dossier Kal)

history.text: Otto III was born in the Ketil wood, on the road between Noviomagus and Xanten.
history.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon (dossier Th)

history.text: On 15 June the empress Theophanu died here. She was buried at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne.
history.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon (dossier Th)

history.text: In 996 and 997 Count Balderik and Adela of Hamaland were heard here before Otto III over the abbey of Elten.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts (dossier VP)

history.text: On 16 March a great synod here excommunicated Count Otto of Hammerstein and his wife Irmingard, and ruled from an old book that the chalice stands to the right of the host. On 6 April, at the Easter court, Bishop Adalbold and the merchants of Tiel complained of Count Dirk's toll. The army sent against him was beaten at Vlaardingen on 29 July.
history.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon; nl.wikipedia Slag bij Vlaardingen (1018); Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20-21 as cited in Design/content/realms/frisia_lotharingia.md (dossier Th, SV)

history.text: About 1030-1040 the eight-sided chapel was built in the palace after the pattern of Aachen: tuff, and reused Roman tiles stamped by the Tenth Legion. Some date it 996, some after 1047.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Sint-Nicolaaskapel (Nijmegen); de.wikipedia Valkhof (dossier NK, DV)

history.text: At Pentecost Henry, the emperor's son, wedded Gunhild, daughter of King Cnut, here. She took the name Kunigunde and was crowned on 29 June.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts; en.wikipedia Gunhilda of Denmark (dossier VP, Gun)

history.text: The palace was burned in Duke Godfrey the Bearded's rising against Henry III. Who set the fire is not certain.
history.source: nl.wikipedia Valkhofpalts; de.wikipedia Valkhof (dossier VP, DV)

eras.text: A building yard on a hill. Masons and carpenters work inside the old fort; the king has not been seen here since 777. The cellarer buys little and slowly, the bank settlement lives off the works, and news from court comes by letter.

The old king's Lents. In 806 and 808 Charles comes by ship with his whole house, laws are written in the palace, and for forty days every boat on the Waal has a buyer. An exiled English king passes through in 808.

Louis's house: hunts in the Ketil wood, oaths sworn in May, an assembly that waits for a Dane who does not come. From 834 the emperor arrives after each raid downriver, too late, and holds inquiries. A merchant with a count or a bishop to speak for him can win the emperor's own letter here.

A fort more than a palace. Lothar's men watch the river; in 846 Dorestad burns and nothing is done. Courts are few. In 870 a western king and a Danish count make their bargain in the hall. Burned people come up the river and stay.

The Northmen's winter. Their ships lie under the hill, a rampart of earth and timber rings the palace, and a king's army sits outside in the frost and cannot get in. At the thaw they burn it all and go.

A burned shell slowly mended. Black beams, a few roofs made good, the bank settlement back west of the hill. Kings pass and seldom stay. What Dorestad used to do is now done at Tiel, lower down the Waal.

The Saxon kings' house. Tiel leads the river trade and Noviomagus follows it. Otto holds an assembly here; the child Otto III is here often with his mother, and in 991 the empress Theophanu dies in the palace. Counts and abbesses bring their quarrels. In 1006 and 1007 fleets are on the Waal again and Tiel burns (as places/traiectum.json has it (?)); burned-out Tiel men set up sheds against the old wall here.

The Salian courts. An eight-sided chapel of tuff stands in the palace yard; the emperor comes most years; in 1036 a daughter of King Cnut is married here at Pentecost. English and Rhineland silver pass on the bank.
Burned again in the duke's rising of 1047. The chapel stands among scorched walls. The settlement by the river trades on, with one eye on the counts at the river mouths.

sites.name: The landing under the hill
sites.see: A shelving bank of grey mud and gravel at the foot of a steep hill, boats drawn up bow first, a few oak posts to tie to. Behind, a path climbs through alder and bramble to old stone walls on the skyline. The river is wide and brown and loud at the bend; it smells of wet rope, fish scales and wood smoke.
sites.source: the landing at the hill's foot, a harbour since Roman times: de.wikipedia Valkhof (dossier DV). Nothing is recorded of pilots here: the pilot is the ferryman's invented side work (?)

sites.name: The bank below the wall
sites.see: Trestles and upturned baskets on trodden ground between the river and a high wall of grey-brown tuff. Farm wives from the Batua side with cheese and eels, a potter's boy with Rhine pots in straw, sacks of grain under a hide. When the court is in, the crowd is thick and palace servants push to the front; when it is not, six people and a dog.
sites.source: invented in detail; merchants, boatmen, craftsmen and farmers in a small settlement on the bank (dossier Canon). No market right, fair or toll is recorded: it is a selling place by custom only

sites.name: The old wall of tuff
sites.see: A Roman wall, thick and higher than two men, running along the bank: soft grey stone gone green at the foot, with courses of flat red tile. Lean-to sheds of wattle stand against it. Jackdaws nest in the holes where beams once went. Broken tiles underfoot, some with letters pressed into them.
sites.source: the 4th-century riverside wall of tuff, a stretch of which survives at the Waalkade (dossier MG, GN); the sheds are invented

sites.name: The fort gate
sites.see: At the top of the path an old ditch, half filled, and a gap in a Roman wall closed by a new oak gate. Two spearmen with round shields lean in the shade. Through the gate: scaffolding poles, a heap of cut stone, a white stone capital lying on its side in the straw. Carts wait. A huntsman comes up the hill with a roe deer on a pole.
sites.source: the Roman fort with its ditches, inside which the palace stood (dossier VP); three Corinthian capitals of Carrara marble, about 775-800 (dossier VP). The gate and its guard are invented

sites.name: The king's house
sites.see: A long stone hall inside the old fort, its roof timbers new, its far end still under scaffolding in the first years. Benches along the walls, a raised seat at the east end, hangings where the plaster is unfinished. From the door the whole flat Batua lies open to the north, the river bright across it. It smells of lime, rushes and roast meat on a feast day.
sites.source: the palace of 777, 'a palace of vast size and wonderful work' (Regino 881); the view over the Betuwe (dossier VP, Reg). What it looked like is not known: no ground plan survives, and this picture is invention (?)

sites.name: The clerks' bench
sites.see: A small room off the hall with one window to the south. A sloped desk, a bench, horns of ink, a knife, a stack of wax tablets tied with cord, a chest with an iron lock. A young clerk with inky fingers reads a law aloud to himself to find where the scribe before him went wrong. Chalk dust and the smell of sheepskin.
sites.source: the clerks of the capitularies written here in 806 and 808 (dossier Cap806, Cap808); the room is invented

sites.name: The church by the palace
sites.see: A plain small hall on the slope below the fort, stone to the height of a man and timber above, with a thatched roof and a wooden cross on the gable. Inside it is dark: one lamp, a stone altar, a painted cloth. Old people of the bank stand at the back. To the west the ground is lumpy with graves nobody tends.
sites.source: the parish church by the palace, by tradition Nijmegen's first, of Saint Stephen or Saint Gertrude (the sources disagree), a modest hall of stone or wood; first mentioned in the 15th century and never found (dossier GK, Kal) (?). The grave fields closed about 700 (dossier GN)

sites.name: The king's cellar and barns
sites.see: Inside the fort wall, a stone-footed barn and a sunk cellar with a ramp for casks. Tally sticks hang in bundles from a beam. A heavy man with keys at his belt counts sacks as they come off a cart, and counts them again. Cool air, the sour smell of wine lees, mice.
sites.source: invented; farms of the later Realm of Nijmegen and the forest toward Xanten fed the court (dossier Canon, Ket). No steward of Nijmegen is named in the sources

sites.name: Wendilgard's ale-house
sites.see: A low house of posts and wattle west of the hill, the door facing the river, a bush on a pole above it. One room, a hearth in the middle with the smoke going out through the thatch, benches, a board scratched for a game. Boatmen with wet leg bindings. A broad woman ladles ale from a tub and listens to everything.
sites.source: invented; the settlement of the 9th and 10th centuries lay west of the hill near the river (dossier GN). The house is kept by her daughters and theirs after her

sites.name: The barge bank
sites.see: Downstream of the landing, a flat-bottomed barge half built on blocks, its oak bottom planks wider than a man's chest. Two men with adzes, a boy boiling moss and tar in an iron pot. Split logs stacked to season, a log boat hauled out with a cracked side. Chips everywhere, and the sweet sharp smell of cut oak.
sites.source: invented; river craft of the Rhine branches (Design/content/ships.md); the capitulary of 808 has a heading on the ships ordered built (dossier Cap808)

sites.name: The Batua crossing
sites.see: A broad punt on a pole, grounded where a cart track comes down to the water. Across the brown river the far bank is a low green line of willow and reed, with cattle on it and nothing higher than a hayrick as far as the eye goes. A net dries on stakes. The ferryman sits mending it and watches the current, not you.
sites.source: invented; the Waal 'washes the south side of the island of the Batavians' (Einhard 17, Turner 1880); fishermen in the settlement (dossier GN)

sites.name: The Northmen's rampart
sites.see: A bank of fresh earth and a fence of sharpened timber round the whole hilltop, the palace roofs behind it. Long ships drawn up under the hill where the landing was, shields along their sides. Snow on the ground, smoke from many fires, and across the frozen fields the tents of a king's army that cannot get in.
sites.source: 'a very strong rampart and walls' round Nijmegen, the hard winter and the failed siege: Annales Fuldenses 880; Regino 881 (dossier AF, Reg). No leader of these Northmen is named

sites.name: The king's house, mended
sites.see: The old fort walls, and inside them a hall with new roofs on fire-blackened stone. In the Saxon kings' time it is whole again and hung with cloth; from about 1030 an eight-sided chapel of grey tuff stands in the yard, with red Roman tiles in its walls. After 1047 the hall is a scorched shell once more and only the chapel has a roof.
sites.source: burned 881, in use again by 898, courts of the Ottonian and Salian kings, the chapel about 1030-1040, burned 1047 (dossier Reg, Kal, VP, NK, DV). How and when it was rebuilt is not recorded (?). The chapel's dedication to Saint Nicholas is first written in 1470

people.name: Ratbert
people.trait: Keeper of a larder for a guest who may come this year or in ten: patient, exact, and unable to pass a sack without lifting it.
people.want: The cellar full a month before the court and not a day sooner; sellers who come back with the same measure twice.
people.fear: The king's ship at the bend and the wine not yet in; an envoy asking where last year's oats went.
people.voice: Slow and loud, counts in casks and modii, calls every merchant 'friend' until the price is said.
people.looks: Near fifty, broad and heavy, bald on top with a grey fringe, a clean-shaven jowl, an undyed wool tunic with wine stains, a ring of iron keys and a bundle of tally sticks at his belt.
knows: when the court is expected, a moon before anyone on the river
what the palace table lacks this season
the king's measure and the lawful price of grain after 806
which counts are in the house on a feast, and in what temper
who on the Rhine sells wine that is what he says it is

ties.note: Two stewards who trust each other's tallies and nobody else's; they send word of what each house lacks.
Seats and feeds the count when he comes to the king's house; knows what gift would please him.
The clerk writes down what the cellarer would sooner keep in his head.
Owes the huntsman for game taken on trust all one winter.
Bought a cargo of Thiadbod's wine once. Once.
Orders the larder's hooks, knives and nails from the Deventer smith, and pays late.
Buys Rhine wine by the cask from the same Cologne house each autumn.
gives her spent malt and old casks; she tells him who is selling short
takes his fish on fast days by a custom nobody wrote down
paid him ahead for a vintage that failed, and is still owed six casks
Liutwin's is the Cologne house he has bought from every autumn for twenty years

lines.greet: A boat from Dorestad. Good. What have you got, what does it weigh, and is it the king's measure or your own?
lines.greet_again: You again, friend. The last lot was what you said it was. That is rarer than pepper. Come into the cool.
rumour: The king keeps Lent here, they write. Forty days of fish for three hundred mouths. Bring eels, bring salmon, bring salt.
Count Folcbert is in the house for the feast. He likes hounds better than merchants. I only tell you what I see.
Since the law was made here, wheat is six pennies the measure and no more. Do not let me hear you asked eight.
lines.saying: When the king hunts, sell salt. When the king fasts, sell fish.
lines.farewell: Go well. Come back before the court does, not after. After, I have no time and you have no price.

people.source: invented; the court as the place's one great buyer, and the price caps of 806 (dossier section 4, Cap806). No steward or cellarer of Nijmegen is named in any source

people.name: Engilbald
people.trait: A clerk of the palace, schooled at court under the English master: quick, a little vain of his Latin, starved of talk between courts.
people.want: News, letters to copy, and someone on this hill who can answer a riddle.
people.fear: A wrong word in a law that goes out under the king's name; being left here when the court moves on, as he has been.
people.voice: Fast and precise, drops a Latin word and at once gives it in plain speech; asks questions he already knows the answer to.
people.looks: Late twenties, thin, tonsured, a long nose, ink on the right hand to the knuckle, a plain dark tunic, a case of wax tablets and a bone stylus on a cord round his neck.
knows: the laws made here, word for word, and what they mean for a seller
the riddle of the river and the fish, and the riddles Alcuin wrote for the king's son Pippin
how a charter is dated and witnessed, and what the one of 777 gave to Utrecht
the tally of the Saxon hostages of 785 and where each was sent
who came to the king and why, a season later than it happened
what a book is worth and who is asking for one

ties.note: Alcuin taught him at the court school; he still gets a letter now and then, and reads it to anyone who will listen.
Thinks the cellarer's tally sticks are a way of not being read.
The only other man here with letters; they argue about Easter reckoning for pleasure.
They send each other riddles by any boat that passes between the two houses.
Keeps in the palace chest the tally of the Saxon hostages of 785, her son among them (invented). Nobody has yet asked him for it.
Copies for the bishop of Utrecht what the king's chest holds touching Saint Martin's lands.
takes his tallies for the palace and mends his Latin without being asked
reads the count's letters to those who decide, and has had no answer to give him
the ferryman handed over the hostages of 785; the clerk keeps the tally (invented)
tells the abbey's steward a week ahead what the court will want (?)
a clerk up the river whose tallies and his never quite agree
copies for the abbot of Saint-Denis, and is paid in letters

lines.greet: A merchant. Can you read? No? Then listen, it is nearly as good, and I have had nobody to read to since the thaw.
lines.greet_again: You came back. Sit. I have a new one, and you still owe me an answer for the last.
rumour: My master wrote riddles for the king's son. What is a ship? A wandering house, a lodging anywhere. You of all men should have had that.
A king of the English came in Lent with no kingdom. He went on to Rome. They say Rome is good for that.
The law says a double cloak is twenty shillings at most, and half the fine to whoever tells. Look to your neighbours, cloth seller.
lines.saying: A house that is never quiet and a guest who never speaks, and both run together. You crossed it this morning.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and bring me a letter from anywhere. I am not particular.

people.source: invented; the clerks of the capitularies of 806 and 808 (dossier section 3). Alcuin's Disputatio Pippini cum Albino holds riddles, among them the ship; Symphosius 12, Flumen et piscis (texts_793.json symphosius_12_flumen). The rendering of the ship riddle is ours, from memory of the Latin (?)

people.name: Liudrad
people.trait: A Frisian priest schooled at Utrecht, set over a king's church that sees the king one year in ten: kind, tired, good with the dying.
people.want: Wax, oil, and a roof that does not drip on the altar; the poor of the bank fed in Lent.
people.fear: The old graves west of the church, which his people still visit with cups after dark; the day the court finds his Latin thin.
people.voice: Dry and gentle, a Frisian's short sentences; says 'the blessed Martin' as if he were a neighbour upriver.
people.looks: About forty, lean, weathered, tonsured with brown hair going grey, a patched dark tunic, bare feet in summer, a small wooden cross and a knife on the same cord.
knows: who on the bank is hungry, sick or lying
the fasts and feasts, and what may be sold on them
who lies in the old grave field, by family
the road and the river to Utrecht, and who there will lodge a man
what the law of 806 says each lord owes his own poor

ties.note: Liudger taught him his letters at Utrecht before he went east; Liudrad still keeps a psalter leaf in his hand.
Sends to the bishop at Utrecht for chrism and advice, though whose diocese this hill lies in he is not sure (?).
Lets the clerk win arguments and keeps the better wine.
She feeds his poor on the days he cannot; he does not ask where the bread came from.
Taught the Saxon his prayers again, slowly, without anyone holding a sword.
The priest of the upper church at Dorestad was at school with him.

lines.greet: God keep you. You came up the hill for the palace and found a church. Most do it the other way round.
lines.greet_again: The shipman. Your candle burned to the end. I watched it. Somebody ought to.
rumour: There are more poor on the road each week. The law says each lord feeds his own. The road has no lord.
Old women still carry a cup to the graves at the dark of the year. I bless the cup. It seems the lesser sin.
When the court comes the church is full of silk. When it goes, it is me and nine fishermen. God counts both.
lines.saying: A hill the height of thirty men is a mountain to a Frisian. I get my breath back and call it prayer.
lines.farewell: Go safely. Say a word for us at Saint Martin's if you pass Utrecht.

people.source: invented; the parish church by the palace (dossier GK) and the clause of 806 that each lord feeds his own poor (dossier Cap806). No priest of Nijmegen is named; the diocese is unchecked (?)

people.name: Wendilgard
people.trait: A boatman's widow who brews for the bank and lodges whoever the river brings: remembers every face, every debt and what each man said he was carrying.
people.want: Barley at a fair price, her two daughters married to men with boats, and the masons paid so they can pay her.
people.fear: A court that stays forty days and drinks on the king's word; fire in the thatch.
people.voice: Warm and blunt, laughs before she finishes; says a price once.
people.looks: Mid thirties, broad, strong forearms, red hair under a linen cloth, a brown gown kilted up, a wooden ladle in her hand and a small silver cross a guest once left in pledge.
knows: who is on the river this week, and what they carry
which boatmen are worth hiring and which drink their pay
what the palace servants say when they think nobody listens
the price of barley and malt on both banks
where a stranger can sleep dry

ties.note: The ferryman is her dead husband's brother; he brings fish, she brings him his sense.
Feeds his poor from the bottom of the pot.
The cellarer lets her have spent malt and old casks; she tells him who is selling short.
The Maas-mouth pilot lodged here a winter when the ice shut the river, and paid in stories.
Buys her barley through the Dorestad widow's storehouse in thin years, and pays on the day.
A cousin by marriage who brews by the landing on the IJssel; they send each other yeast and bad news.
an ale-wife up the Rhine who has something to say about bog myrtle

lines.greet: In from the wet. Sit there, not there, that is Eilward's. Ale is ale here. We do not have the other kind.
lines.greet_again: I know you. Four men, a small boat, and you paid. Sit where you like.
rumour: The masons were not paid at Martinmas. They drink on a tally now. A king's house, built on my ale.
A man from Dorestad was asking after you. Big ship, soft voice, gave my girls a comb each. I did not like him.
The court is coming, the cellarer says. He has said it every spring since I was married.
lines.saying: Better a guest who pays in pennies than a lord who pays in thanks.
lines.farewell: Mind the bend below the wall. And bring barley next time, if you want to be loved.

people.source: invented; the bank settlement of boatmen and craftsmen (dossier Canon, GN). The soft-voiced man is the spine's rival, cast.thiadbod

people.name: Eilward
people.trait: Ferryman and fisherman of the Batua crossing: has read one river all his life and trusts nothing that stands still.
people.want: A second punt, a boy to pole it, and the palace to stop asking for fish he has not caught yet.
people.fear: The spring flood that takes the bank and his nets with it; king's men who want a crossing and call it service.
people.voice: Few words, all of them about water; calls the river 'she' and the palace 'up there'.
people.looks: Early twenties in 793, long-armed, sunburnt, fair hair tied back, a short Frisian cloak, bare legs, an eel spear and a pole twice his height.
knows: where the Waal runs deep this year and where she has moved
the parting of the streams upriver at Herispich, and which branch has water
what came down the river last night
the Batua farms and what they sell at the door
the answer to the clerk's riddle, though nobody has asked him

ties.note: His brother's widow; he eats at her fire and mends her roof.
Gerlef showed him how to keep marks in his head the winter the old pilot was iced in here.
Trades fish for venison across the palace's back, and neither speaks of it.
Owes the palace fish each fast day, by custom nobody wrote down.
Says the IJssel men cannot read brown water. Thancric has his own word for the Waal.
Was once made to pay the tenth at Dorestad on his own supper.
a boatman of the Ruhr mouth; they trade poles and lies at the Christmas reckoning

lines.greet: You came up on the south side. Good. She has a bar on the north this year that was not there at Easter.
lines.greet_again: The small boat. You sit her well in the bend. Somebody taught you, or she did.
rumour: Upriver where the two streams part, the Rhine has the water this summer. Go by the Waal and you will pole half of it.
Three boats came down in the night without a light. Laden. Nobody up there asked. I do not ask either.
The clerk asked me what runs and never tires. I said I knew it but it was Lent and I was fishing.
lines.saying: A river tells you everything twice. The second time is the flood.
lines.farewell: Keep to the outside of the bend. If she turns brown and quick, tie up and wait.

people.source: invented; fishermen and boatmen of the settlement (dossier GN, Canon); the parting of Rhine and Waal at Herispich (Regino 885). Nothing is recorded of bars or shoals here: his are invented (?)

people.name: Haribrand
people.trait: A Saxon carried west with his kin in the king's war and set to keep the king's wood: silent, sure-footed, baptised by order and not yet decided about it.
people.want: Word of his brother, taken on another road; to be left alone among the trees.
people.fear: The hunt going badly on the one day in ten years the king rides; being moved again.
people.voice: Slow Frankish with a Saxon's broad vowels; answers a question with what the wood did this morning.
people.looks: Mid twenties in 797, tall, rangy, light brown hair cut short as the Franks ordered, a green-grey tunic, leather leggings, a boar spear, two lean hounds at heel.
knows: the Ketil wood from here to Xanten: paths, springs, where the boar lie
when a hunt is ordered, before the cellarer does
which Saxons were settled where along the river
hounds, hides and hawks, and what each is worth to a lord
what the gate guards let through for a haunch

ties.note: The one priest who taught him without a sword in the room.
Venison for fish, and no questions.
Brings game to the cellar; is owed for a winter of it.
Finds the boar when the count hunts here, and has seen what puts him in a giving mood.
Liudger knew his father's hall east of the IJssel and asks after the family when he passes.
The Saxon alewife at Deventer passes word between the families carried west and those left at home.
keeps the emperor's wood and his hounds, and is asked after before the counts are

lines.greet: You are from the river. I am from further off. The boar are in the low wood today, if that is what you came about.
lines.greet_again: The shipman. The hounds know you now. That took them less time than it took me.
rumour: The count hunts here at the feast. Give him a hound that will hold a boar and he will give you his ear.
They moved a third of my people out of our land. I was fifteen. My brother went by another road. I ask every boat.
The king has not ridden this wood since before I came. I keep it as if he came tomorrow. That is the work.
lines.saying: The wood does not care who is king. It is the one thing here that does not.
lines.farewell: If you pass a Saxon on the Rhine with a scar through his left brow, say Haribrand keeps the Ketil wood.

people.source: invented; the king's hunting in the forest from Nijmegen to Xanten (dossier Ket, ARF 817, 825); Saxons carried off and settled in Francia in the last years of the war (Annales regni Francorum 795-804, Einhard c. 7; the spine's thread saxon_end)

people.name: Louis
people.trait: The emperor, Charles's son: devout, courteous, a great hunter, quick to forgive and slow to arrive.
people.want: The coast watched, his sons at peace, and the truth of what happened downriver from someone who was there.
people.fear: His own sons; that each fleet on the Rhine is a judgement on him.
people.voice: Quiet and exact, asks before he speaks, thanks a merchant as he would a count and forgets neither.
people.looks: In his forties and fifties, strongly built, long-armed, a long nose, hair cut short, a plain blue cloak over a gold-bordered tunic for the feast and hunting green otherwise, a small gold cross, a boar spear never far off.
knows: what his counts have told him of the raids, which is less than a skipper saw
who holds each river mouth by his gift, and on what oath
the letter he gives his own merchants, and what he asks for it each May
the Ketil wood, better than any man but his huntsman

ties.note: His count on Walcheren, killed holding the island in 837 while the emperor was still on the road here.
Waited here a whole assembly in 827 for Godfrid's son Horik, who had promised to come and did not.
Sent the monk north with the baptised Dane Harald, and hears from him seldom.
Gave Rorik and his brother Dorestad to hold against other Northmen; what that oath is worth is his sons' problem.
Knows his huntsman by name and asks after the hounds before he asks after the counts.
his arch-chaplain, in most years his own man

lines.greet: You are a merchant of the river. Speak plainly. I hear enough from counts who were not there.
lines.greet_again: I know your face. You told me the truth once when it was unwelcome. Do it again.
rumour: I came as fast as the river allowed. They had gone. They are always gone.
My counts say the Frisians would not fight. The Frisians say nobody led them. You were there. Which did you see?
A beam fell on me at Aachen in Holy Week. I came here to hunt. God spares a man for a reason, or to warn him.
lines.saying: A king hears everything late. A merchant hears it early and sells it.
lines.farewell: Go in peace. Be here in May with what is owed my chamber.

people.source: real: Louis the Pious (778-840), emperor from 814, here in 817, 821, 825, 827, 830, 837 and 838: Annales regni Francorum; Annales Bertiniani (dossier ARF, AB). The fall of the portico in Holy Week 817 and the hunt here after it: ARF 817. His looks follow Thegan's Life of Louis c. 19, from memory (?). His words are invented. He is met only in the years the annals put him here

people.name: Eberhard
people.trait: A count's son held by the Northmen in the palace they have taken: young, proud, counting the days by the frost.
people.want: Word carried to his mother Evesa that he lives and what is asked for him.
people.fear: That the king's army will go home before the price is paid, and the ships will take him north at the thaw.
people.voice: Short and stiff, a lord's son trying not to ask a favour of a merchant.
people.looks: A young Saxon nobleman, tall, fair, unshaven, a good red tunic gone filthy, no belt and no sword, a rope round one ankle, breath smoking in the cold.
knows: how many ships lie under the hill and how the rampart is kept
what the Northmen will take for him, and that they keep such bargains
that they mean to burn the palace when they go
who his mother is and where she can be found with silver

ties.note: The Deventer merchant carried part of the ransom his mother Evesa paid 'at a great price' (Regino 881). Where she lived is not recorded: the game puts her on the IJssel (?).
No friend to any Northman holding a Frankish river, sworn or not.

lines.greet: You trade with them. I do not blame you, it is winter. Will you carry a message out with your empty sacks?
lines.greet_again: You came back through the rampart. Then she has an answer. Say it quickly, they are watching.
rumour: They count silver by weight and they count it well. My mother must not send light coin. Tell her.
The king sits out there in the snow. He will not get in. They know it and he is beginning to.
When they go they will burn this. They said it at meat, laughing. It is the king's house. I ate at that table as a boy.
lines.saying: A hall is whoever sits in it.
lines.farewell: Go. If I come out of this, the house of Meginhard will know your name.

people.source: real: Eberhard the Saxon, son of Count Meginhard, taken captive at Nijmegen and ransomed by his mother Evesa 'at a great price': Regino of Prüm 881 (dossier Reg). His birth and death are not given; whether he is the Evarhard who struck the first blow at Herispich in 885 is a guess (?). His words are invented

people.name: Sibrand
people.trait: A merchant of Tiel, burned out by the fleet of 1006, who keeps a shed against the old wall here and half his heart downriver: hard, funny, loyal to his drinking fellows before any lord.
people.want: The river mouths open and one toll on them, not two; his scale, his wife and his cask of pennies never again in the same boat.
people.fear: Striped sails on the Waal; Count Dirk's fort at Vlaardingen growing a second tower.
people.voice: Quick and dry, swears by his own right hand, prices everything he looks at including you.
people.looks: About forty, short, thick in the shoulder, a clipped dark beard, a good blue cloak pinned with an English silver brooch, a folding scale in a leather case at his belt.
knows: prices at Tiel, at Traiectum and across the sea at London
what Count Dirk takes at the river mouths and from whom
English pennies and Tiel pennies, by weight and by look
who among the river merchants will swear for a man and who will not
what was really said before the emperor at Easter

ties.note: His cousin on the Stathe at Utrecht, who lodged him the winter after Tiel burned.
Not her but her house: he drinks at the ale-house her line still keeps, and pays the whole bench's score on feast days.
Says Deventer pennies are light, like his cousin does, and takes them anyway.
Trades to England under whatever king holds London; under Cnut the tolls on the road to Rome are eased for men like him (?).
the Count Palatine, whose stretch of the river costs more each year
never met the old count: it is his grandson's fort and toll at Vlaardingen that the Tiel men curse before the emperor in 1018

lines.greet: A stranger with a clean boat. Either you are honest or you are new. Sit down, I will find out which.
lines.greet_again: My friend with the small boat. I told the bench you would be back. I had money on it.
rumour: Dirk has a fort at the mouth and takes toll of every keel for England. We pay the king at Tiel. Now we pay twice.
The fleet burned Tiel while the count's men looked for their shoes. I came away with a scale and a wife. Good ones, both.
At Easter we go up the hill with the bishop and say it to the emperor's face. Come and stand with us. It costs nothing but Dirk.
lines.saying: A monk wrote that we Tiel men judge by our own will and not by law. He was not wrong. He was not invited.
lines.farewell: Go well. If they ask at Vlaardingen whose man you are, say nobody's, and say it politely.

people.source: invented; the cousin from Tiel of places/traiectum.json (traiectum.bernbod). Tiel on the Waal led the river trade 925-1050 with Rhineland and English ties, and Nijmegen followed (dossier VvG); the merchants of Tiel complained of Dirk's toll here at Easter 1018 (dossier SV, Th). The burning of Tiel in 1006 and the monk's complaint are Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum I.8 and II.20, from memory (?)

people.name: Dirk
people.trait: Count of the Frisians of the west coast: an old, patient gatherer of land, who comes to the king's house once and leaves it owning what he had only held.
people.want: What he holds in fief made his own for ever, from the river mouths to Texel; an abbey at Egmond rich enough to pray him into heaven.
people.fear: A king grown up enough to ask what was given away in his name when he was five.
people.voice: Slow, courteous, Frisian under the court manners; never names a sum first.
people.looks: A broad white-bearded man near sixty in a fur-lined cloak with a great gold brooch, a ring on every finger of one hand, a chaplain carrying a book behind him.
knows: every toll and landing from the Maas mouth to the Vlie
what the king's charter of August 985 gives him, word for word
who holds the other half of the toll at Medemelacha
what the abbey at Egmond lacks for its altar

ties.note: Count Ansfried was given the king's share of Medemelacha's toll two months before Dirk's own charter; they are polite about it
the old bishop's house claims tithes and tenths on a coast that Dirk counts as his
never met: it is his grandson's toll at Vlaardingen that the Tiel men come up this hill to curse in 1018

lines.greet: A shipman, in the king's house. Then you have come up past my landings. Did my men take the toll, or did they only look as if they would?
lines.greet_again: You again. Good. I like a man who comes twice; a man who comes once has usually taken something.
rumour: The king is five years old and gives land with a steady hand. His mother's hand, but steady.
Between the Lier and the IJssel, and from the stream at Medemelacha to the Kennemer bounds: mine now, and my sons'. The clerks wrote it in August. I had it read to me three times.
Count Ansfried has the king's share of the toll on the Almere, and prays more than he counts. One of us will have the better of that.
lines.saying: Land that is lent is land that is watched. Land that is given can be left alone.
lines.farewell: Go down by my landings again. Pay what they ask. If they ask twice, tell them my name and see what happens.

people.source: historical: Dirk II, count in West Frisia (d. 6 May 988). At Nijmegen on 25 August 985 Otto III gave him in ownership what he had held in fief: the land between the Liora and the Hisla, the villa Sunnimeri, the land between Medemelacha and Chinnelosara gemarchi, and Texla (MGH DD O III no. 19; nl.wikipedia 'Dirk II van Holland'). His grandson Dirk III's toll at Vlaardingen and the battle of 29 July 1018: Alpertus, De diversitate temporum II.20-21. His words are invented.

stories.title: The count at the king's table
stories.summary: At Dorestad the count is behind his steward and his tally. On a feast at the king's house he sits among his equals with a cup in his hand, and a merchant with the right gift can ask him for time to his face.
stories.picture: A long stone hall by rushlight: Frankish lords on benches, a thick-set count in a red cloak turning to look down at a merchant who holds two lean hounds on a leash.

beats.when: year < 840 and debt > 0 and not flag.db_extension
beats.text: Hartwin the steward says, counting aloud, that the count has gone up to the king's house at Noviomagus for the feast, and that the day does not move because the count has.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year < 840 and debt > 0 and not flag.db_extension
beats.text: Ratbert tells what the table lacks and what the count likes: a hound that will hold a boar, a salmon in a fast, good Rhine wine, a hawk. Nothing that looks like payment.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year >= 797 and year < 836 and not flag.db_extension
beats.text: Haribrand, who finds the boar for the count, will say which morning the hunt went well. That is the evening to ask.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and feast and year < 840 and debt > 0 and not flag.db_extension
beats.text: The gift is carried in before the company. The count must answer where other lords can hear him: he gives a delay past the day, or he names an errand in place of the silver.

beats.when: flag.db_service and year < 813
beats.text: The errand: English hounds and a cloak of the old length, for his table and his back.

endings.how: A gift fit for the company, given on a feast after a good hunt.
endings.text: The count laughs, calls you 'shipman' before the whole bench and gives you until the next Michaelmas. Hartwin cuts a new notch without a word.
endings.reward: flag db_extension: the debt's day moves a year, one time only; Folcbert's feeling rises; Ratbert seats you at the low table on later feasts

endings.how: A poor gift, or the right gift on the wrong evening.
endings.text: He will not be seen to be bought cheap. He names an errand across the sea instead, and half the silver is forgiven when it is done.
endings.reward: flag db_service: an errand to Lundenwic in place of part of the silver; the day stands

endings.how: You came up the hill, looked at the company and went down again.
endings.text: Nothing is asked and nothing is lost but the days. Wendilgard says it was the wiser road, and that Thiadbod's man had been at the gate asking who you spoke to.
endings.reward: news of the rival's interest in the debt; Wendilgard's feeling rises

stories.reward: A year's delay on the Wōkerer's silver, or an errand in its place, and the count knows your face.

stories.title: The house that runs
stories.summary: The palace clerk has a Latin riddle on a wax tablet and nobody to try it on. It is the river and the fish, and the man on the bank who could answer it has never been asked.
stories.picture: A thin clerk at a sloped desk holding out a wax tablet; through the window behind him, far below, a ferryman poling a punt across a wide brown river.

beats.when: year >= 793
beats.text: The schoolmaster at Saint Martin's, once his key is answered, says the next one is with a clerk at the king's house upriver, who was Alcuin's pupil and will talk for a week if let.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and not text.symphosius_12_flumen
beats.text: Engilbald gives the tablet: three lines of Symphosius. It needs Latin: a reader aboard, a monk, or lessons. He tells of the riddles his master wrote for the king's son Pippin.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and text.symphosius_12_flumen
beats.text: Eilward, mending a net, says the house is loud and the guest is dumb and both go the same way, and that he took the clerk's supper out of it this morning.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and riddle.riddle_symphosius_12_flumen
beats.text: The answer given, Engilbald pays as clerks pay: he copies out for you the lawful prices and the words of a charter, and says an English book has the same riddle in English.

endings.how: You answered it yourself, with or without the ferryman.
endings.text: Engilbald is delighted and a little put out. From then on he keeps a riddle and a piece of court news for you each time you lie here.
endings.reward: the riddle's own reward (rw_standing_small); Engilbald's feeling rises; a fresh court rumour at each later visit

endings.how: You told the clerk it was Eilward's answer.
endings.text: The clerk walks down the hill for the first time in a year to ask a fisherman a question. They do not become friends. Eilward gets his fish dues written down and halved.
endings.reward: Eilward's feeling rises sharply: he pilots you on the Waal for nothing; Engilbald's rises a little

endings.how: You sold the tablet on, unanswered, to a school downriver.
endings.text: A few pennies. The clerk hears of it by the next boat and has nothing more to read to you.
endings.reward: a little silver; Engilbald's door is shut for a year

stories.reward: The text symphosius_12_flumen in the chest, a clerk in the palace who tells you the court's news, and the next step on the Latin riddles' road.

stories.title: Six pennies the measure
stories.summary: In Lent of 806 the king is in the palace, the harvest has failed again, and a law is written on this hill saying what grain may cost and what to call a man who buys at harvest to sell dear. A merchant lying below with grain in the hold hears it read before the ink is dry.
stories.picture: A clerk reading from a sheet at the fort gate to a crowd of thin people and a few merchants; behind them a boat at the landing, low in the water with sacks.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 806
beats.text: The law is read aloud: by the modius, oats two pennies, barley three, spelt three, rye four, cleaned wheat six. Who buys at harvest for two to sell at four or six takes shameful gain. Who buys from need, to keep or to share, does trade.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 806 and (hold.wheat > 0 or hold.rye > 0 or hold.barley > 0 or hold.oats > 0)
beats.text: Ratbert will take the whole hold at the lawful price, for the king's table and the king's poor, and pay on the nail. It is less than the bank would give by dusk.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year >= 805 and year <= 807
beats.text: Liudrad asks for nothing. He says the road has no lord, and there are forty on it by the old graves tonight.

beats.when: year >= 806 and year <= 807 and flag.hy_sold_dear
beats.text: Upriver the price is what it is, law or no law. But half a fine goes to whoever tells, and somebody on the quay knew your boat at Noviomagus.

endings.how: You sold to the cellar at the lawful price.
endings.text: A thin profit, paid in good new pennies. Ratbert remembers the measure was full. So does the clerk, who wrote down who sold.
endings.reward: silver at the capped price; Ratbert's feeling rises; first call on the cellar's orders before each later court

endings.how: You gave a share to the priest for the people on the road.
endings.text: Forty people eat for a week. Liudrad says your name at the altar, which nobody on this hill has had done for them since the king was last here.
endings.reward: flag hy_fed_poor; standing in the region rises; Liudrad's feeling rises sharply and the church is sanctuary for you and your crew

endings.how: You kept the hold shut and carried it upriver for the dear price.
endings.text: The silver is real and so is the risk. If you are named, the fine is heavy and the informer is somebody you know.
endings.reward: flag hy_sold_dear; high silver; a doubtful chance of a fine at any Frankish port for a year; Ratbert buys nothing from you until 808

stories.reward: The lawful prices known for good, and one of three men on this hill in your debt.

stories.title: What the fort could see
stories.summary: Three times in forty years the great men come to this hill because of the Northmen, and three times a merchant on the bank sees more than they do: the burning of 846, the bargain of 870, and the winter of 880 when the Northmen sit in the king's own hall.
stories.picture: Night on the fort wall: an emperor in a dark cloak among armed men, all looking west down the river, where the low sky is red.

beats.when: year >= 834 and year <= 846
beats.text: Each raid year the house must choose: bury the silver or carry it. The road upriver to the emperor's fort is the one the frightened take.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 846
beats.text: This year the emperor Lothar is in the fort. Boats come up with burned people in them. He has men, and he does not move. If you saw the fleet at the river mouths and came here first, the gate will hear you.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 870
beats.text: This year King Charles from the west and Rorik the Northman, lord of Dorestad, met in the palace and bound themselves. A merchant who will swear to Rorik's peace can do it here before both.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year >= 880 and year <= 881
beats.text: The Northmen hold the palace behind a new rampart; the king's army freezes outside. Both will buy grain and ale. Inside is a count's son, Eberhard, who wants a message carried to his mother.

beats.when: year >= 880 and year <= 881
beats.text: Evesa has the silver weighed and will not send it with a soldier. She asks what kind of man goes through a rampart twice.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year >= 882 and year < 900
beats.text: They burned it when they left, as the captive said they would. Black stone, new thatch on one end. The ale-house is back in the same place.

endings.how: You took Evesa's silver through the rampart and brought her son out.
endings.text: Eberhard walks out over the frozen ditch. The house of Meginhard does not forget it: your heirs have a lord's word on the IJssel and the lower Rhine.
endings.reward: a large payment from Evesa; a friend that passes to your heir; lodging and a hearing in any hall of Meginhard's kin

endings.how: In 870 you swore to Rorik's peace before the two lords.
endings.text: You pay the Dane's toll and his ships pass you by. Franks upriver call you his man, some of them to your face.
endings.reward: flag df_rorik_man; Rorik's ships do not stop you while he lives; a colder welcome at Frankish halls

endings.how: In the winter of 880 you sold to the camp and to the army and carried no message.
endings.text: Good silver, by weight, from both sides of the ditch. At the thaw the palace burns and the ships go north with whoever was not ransomed.
endings.reward: high silver; the priest of the bank and the Saxon houses remember it against you

endings.how: In 846 you reached the fort before the smoke did and told what you had seen.
endings.text: The emperor does nothing with it. But the bank does: boats are hidden, the church plate goes inland, and afterwards the bank knows who told them.
endings.reward: flag df_warned; standing in the region rises; free lodging at the ale-house for the house's lifetime

stories.reward: A lord's house in your debt, or a Dane's peace, or silver from both sides of a ditch: and whichever it is, the next heir inherits it.

stories.title: The toll at the river mouth
stories.summary: At Easter 1018 the emperor Henry is at Noviomagus, and the merchants of Tiel come up the Waal with the bishop of Utrecht to complain that Count Dirk has built a fort at Vlaardingen and takes toll of every ship bound for England. They want a known house to speak with them.
stories.picture: The mended hall at Easter: an emperor and empress seated, a bishop standing, and before them a knot of river merchants in good cloaks, one pushed forward to speak.

beats.when: year = 1018
beats.text: In Lent the bishop's men ask every house that sails by the river mouths what Count Dirk took from it last season, and whether it will say so aloud.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 1018 and feast
beats.text: On Easter day Sibrand and the Tiel men make the complaint before the emperor, the bishop beside them. A merchant who speaks is heard and remembered: by the emperor, and by the count's friends in the hall.

beats.when: moored and port.id = noviomagus and year = 1018
beats.text: An army is ordered against the count. It will go by water, and ships are wanted to carry it down to the mouths before Lammas.

beats.when: year = 1018
beats.text: After Saint James's day the news comes along the coast: the emperor's army went into the ditches at Vlaardingen and did not come out. The toll stands.

beats.when: year = 1036 and month >= 5 and month <= 6
beats.text: Eighteen years on, the river mouths are open to English keels again: at Pentecost the emperor's son weds a daughter of King Cnut in this house, and English and Danish hulls lie along the bank with the bride's silver in them.

endings.how: You spoke for the merchants and kept your ship out of the levy.
endings.text: The emperor's chamber knows your house; so does Count Dirk. You pay his toll in full ever after, and are searched for it.
endings.reward: standing with the Frankish realm rises; a seat among the river merchants at their yearly drinking; Dirk's toll is never eased for you

endings.how: You spoke, and lent your ship to carry the army.
endings.text: Paid hire, and a doubtful chance of coming back with the ship. Those who do come back are owed by the bishop for a generation.
endings.reward: hire silver; the bishop of Utrecht stands surety for the house; a doubtful loss of the ship at Vlaardingen

endings.how: You held your tongue in the hall and sent the count word of what was said.
endings.text: The Tiel men stop drinking with you. At Vlaardingen your ship is waved through at half the toll, and the count's steward knows your name.
endings.reward: half toll at the river mouths while Dirk lives; the river merchants' feeling falls

stories.reward: A standing with the emperor's chamber or with the count at the river mouths: not both.

works.name: A hard of your own at the landing
works.what: Oak piles and a bed of brushwood and gravel on the mud under the hill, so a boat can lie and load dry-shod at any height of the river.
works.needs: The cellarer's goodwill, since the bank under the hill is the king's; and a season when the river is low.
works.gives: Loading and unloading here take half the time; porters cost less; the boat is safe from the spring flood while you are up the hill.
works.picture: Men driving oak piles into grey river mud with a great wooden maul, a small boat waiting off the bank, the hill and its walls behind.
works.source: invented in the period's manner; the landing at the hill's foot was a harbour from Roman times (dossier DV); timber-and-brushwood hards as at Dorestad (works_793.json) (?)

works.name: A store against the old wall
works.what: A lean-to of oak posts and wattle built against the Roman wall of tuff on the bank, with a raised floor and a door that bars.
works.needs: A plot agreed with the cellarer, and to be known on the bank: no stranger builds against the king's wall.
works.gives: Goods can be left here between courts and sold when the court comes and the price is highest; no store rent at Noviomagus.
works.picture: A new wattle shed with a thatched lean-to roof against a high grey Roman wall with red tile courses; a man hanging its door.
works.source: invented; the riverside wall of tuff, a stretch of which still stands (dossier MG, GN). Burned with everything else in 881 and to be built again by the heir

works.name: A table for the poor in Lent
works.what: Bread, pease and salt fish given at the church door through the forty days, in your house's name, as the law of 806 says each lord must do for his own.
works.needs: To be here, or to leave the silver with the priest, before Ash Wednesday.
works.gives: Standing in the region rises; the priest speaks for you; your crew's hearts lift when they hear it said at Mass. In the famine years it counts double.
works.picture: A church door on a cold morning: a priest and an alewife ladling from a pot to a line of ragged people, a merchant standing to one side.
works.source: the capitulary of Nijmegen, March 806: each lord feeds his own poor (dossier Cap806); the table itself is invented

works.name: A bell for the church by the palace
works.what: A small cast bronze bell hung in a timber frame by the church door, to call the bank to Mass and to ring when the river rises in the night.
works.needs: Copper and tin brought here by you, and a founder fetched from the Rhine or the Maas.
works.gives: The priest's lasting friendship; your dead are named here every year; the bank is warned of flood and, in the raid years, of ships.
works.picture: A bronze bell the size of a bucket hanging in a rough oak frame beside a thatched church, a priest with his hand on the rope.
works.source: invented in the period's manner; bells were wanted for the Frisian churches in these years (the spine's cast.liudger) (?)

works.name: Stone for the eight-sided chapel
works.what: A boatload of tuff from the Rhine and old red tile dug from the Roman ruins, given to the works of the new chapel in the palace yard.
works.needs: A river ship that can carry stone, and leave from the master of the works.
works.gives: The emperor's chamber knows your house: a hearing at the Easter court without a lord to speak for you.
works.picture: Masons on a scaffold raising an eight-sided wall of grey stone banded with red tile; a barge of cut blocks at the foot of the hill.
works.source: the chapel of about 1030-1040, tuff and reused Roman tiles stamped by the Tenth Legion (dossier NK, DV); the gift is invented. Its date is disputed (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter, or hired with its crew by the trip
ships.note: The palace's own carrying is done in flat-bottomed barges, poled down and towed up: grain, wine casks, stone for the works. The wrights on the bank build nothing else as well.
ships.picture: A long flat-bottomed barge with square ends, low in the brown water under a load of casks, two men poling.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md (flat-bottomed river transports of the Rhine); the yard here is invented

ships.note: The cheapest thing that will carry a cargo between the river towns: a widened oak log with planks added. Boatmen sell them when a court ends and the work goes.
ships.picture: A long narrow boat hollowed from one oak with a plank added along each side, hauled out on the mud.
ships.source: story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_logboat_expanded (250 d at any landing on the Rhine branches); Design/content/ships.md

ships.how: bought second-hand, or built in a fortnight
ships.note: The ferryman's kind of boat: for crossing to the Batua farms and buying at the door, or for lightering goods to the bank when the river is low.
ships.picture: A small flat punt with a man standing in the stern on a long pole, reeds behind.

ships.note: The fishermen of the bank work the Waal in small plank boats; one comes up for sale when a man dies or goes to the palace's service.
ships.picture: A small open plank boat with two oars and a net heaped in the bow, drawn up beside drying stakes.
ships.source: fishermen in the settlement (dossier GN); Design/content/ships.md

ships.how: bought second-hand from the palace when an old one is laid aside (seldom, and only by a house the cellarer trusts)
ships.note: Kings came here by water: Charles down the Moselle and Rhine in 806, Louis down the Maas in 821. The ships that carry a court's baggage grow old like any others.
ships.picture: A broad river ship with a tent amidships and a carved stem, moored under the hill with palace servants carrying chests ashore.
ships.source: Annales regni Francorum 806, 821 (dossier ARF); that the palace sold off old ships is invented (?)

sayings.text: Whoever buys grain or wine at harvest for two pennies and keeps it until it sells for four or six: that we call shameful gain. Whoever buys from need, to keep for himself or to share with others: that we call trade.
sayings.source: Capitulary of Nijmegen, March 806 (MGH Capit. I no. 46), in the dossier's own rendering of the Latin

sayings.text: The king began a palace at Nimeguen, on the Waal, the stream that washes the south side of the island of the Batavians.
sayings.source: Einhard, Life of Charlemagne c. 17, tr. S. E. Turner 1880, lightly shortened

sayings.text: A palace of vast size and wonderful work.
sayings.source: Regino of Prüm, Chronicon, year 881, in the dossier's own rendering

sayings.text: What is a ship? A wandering house, a lodging anywhere, a traveller who leaves no track.
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino; our rendering, from memory of the Latin (?)

sayings.text: A house that is never quiet and a guest who never speaks, and both run together.
sayings.source: Symphosius, Aenigmata 12, Flumen et piscis (texts_793.json symphosius_12_flumen); our plain rendering of the gist

sayings.text: The old king called the short Frisian cloaks napkins: no use in bed, on a horse, or behind a hedge. Then he made a law about the price.
sayings.source: after Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (tr. A. J. Grant 1907), retold not quoted; the price law is the capitulary of Nijmegen, April 808

sayings.text: A perjurer loses his hand, or buys it back. Count your fingers before you swear at Noviomagus.
sayings.source: the first sentence from the capitulary of Nijmegen, April 808 (dossier Cap808); the second invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: When the king hunts, sell salt. When the king fasts, sell fish.
A hill the height of thirty men is a mountain to a Frisian.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the hill is about 35 m high (dossier DV, VP)

sayings.text: We set the benches for the Dane. He did not come. We ate his dinner.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on the assembly of 827 that waited for Horik (Annales regni Francorum 827)

sayings.text: This year the emperor was at Noviomagus and saw Dorestad burn, and it was not avenged.
sayings.source: in the Chronicle's manner, after Annales Xantenses 846; our wording

easter_eggs.text: Broken red tiles in the rubble under the old wall have letters pressed into them: LEG X G. Nobody on the bank can say whose mark it is. It is the Tenth Legion's; two hundred and forty years on, masons will build such tiles into the eight-sided chapel.
easter_eggs.source: reused Roman tiles stamped by the Tenth Legion in the chapel of about 1030 (dossier NK, DV); the stamp's wording as usually read, from memory (?)

easter_eggs.text: A white stone capital carved with leaves lies on its side in straw inside the gate, waiting to be raised. The mason says the stone came from beyond the mountains and cost more than his village.
easter_eggs.source: three Corinthian capitals of Carrara marble, about 775-800, two of them later reused in the 12th-century chapel (dossier VP)

easter_eggs.text: On the bank market a farm wife will sometimes offer a small thick gold coin her husband ploughed up, with a head on one side and NIOMAGO round it. She wants to know if it is money.
easter_eggs.source: gold tremisses reading Niomago in the Escharen hoard of 590-600, very likely struck here (dossier VvG)

easter_eggs.text: West of the church the ground is uneven for a long way. More than two thousand lie there, some with an axe, one with a great lance, one in a cloth with gold thread in it. Nobody has been buried so since the priest's great-grandfather's day.
easter_eggs.source: the grave fields around Mariënburg, closed about 700 (dossier GN, MG)

easter_eggs.text: The clerk will show, if asked nicely, how the king's charters are dated from this house: 'in Niumago palacio publico'. The one he copies it from gave Leusden and four forests to Saint Martin's at Utrecht, sixteen years before the game begins.
easter_eggs.source: the charter of 8 June 777 (dossier VP; Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md)

easter_eggs.text: About 828 the palace librarian Gerward, who has charge of the works here, lodges a night on the Aachen road, hears from his host of a woman healed, will not sleep until he has questioned her himself, and tells the emperor next day. The clerk says he asks every question three ways.
easter_eggs.source: Einhard, Translatio Marcellini et Petri (dossier Trans); the clerk's remark is invented

easter_eggs.text: After the Northmen's winter a fisherman's net brings up an iron sword from the river bed. Along the blade, in inlaid letters: ADALFRIID. He does not know if it is a Northman's or a Frank's, and neither does anyone since.
easter_eggs.source: an iron sword marked ADALFRIID, said to come from the Waal, later 9th century; the museum calls it an 'alleged Viking sword' (dossier VP). The finding is invented

easter_eggs.text: In the summer of 980 a queen on the road from Xanten is brought to bed in the Ketil wood, before she can reach the palace. The child is a king at three and an emperor at fifteen.
easter_eggs.source: Otto III born in the Ketil wood, 980: Thietmar of Merseburg (dossier Th)

easter_eggs.text: A week before Saint John's day in 991 the palace is hung with black: the Greek empress has died in it. Her body goes up the Rhine to Cologne by ship, and every boat on the river gives way.
easter_eggs.source: Theophanu died here 15 June 991 and was buried at Saint Pantaleon, Cologne: Thietmar (dossier Th). The river journey of the body is our guess (?)

easter_eggs.text: At the synod of 1018 an old book is read aloud to settle how the host and the chalice stand on the altar. The chalice goes on the right. A priest on the bank had it wrong for thirty years and nobody was the worse.
easter_eggs.source: Thietmar of Merseburg on the synod of 16 March 1018 (dossier Th); the priest is invented

easter_eggs.text: In 808 a clerk writes the heading 'of the market at the palace' in a list of the king's business and nothing under it. Whatever was decided, nobody on the bank was told.
easter_eggs.source: the capitulary of Nijmegen, April 808, whose headings include the palace market (dossier Cap808); the comment is invented

unlocks.what: A year's delay on the Wōkerer's silver
unlocks.how: Bring a gift fit for the company to the palace on a feast when the count is there, before 840 (the story noviomagus.counts_feast).
unlocks.gives: flag db_extension: one time only for each creditor

unlocks.what: First call on the king's cellar
unlocks.how: Sell Ratbert a full measure twice, or sell at the lawful price in Lent 806.
unlocks.gives: commission: an order from the cellar a moon before each court (fish and salt for Lent, wine and wax for Easter), paid on delivery; news of when the court is coming

unlocks.what: The riddle of the river and the fish, in Latin, on a wax tablet
unlocks.how: Ask at the clerks' bench; it needs a reader aboard, a monk to read it out, or lessons.
unlocks.gives: give_text symphosius_12_flumen (story/unlocks_793.json text.symphosius_12_flumen); it carries riddle_symphosius_12_flumen

unlocks.what: The lawful prices, copied out by a palace clerk
unlocks.how: Answer Engilbald's riddle, or hear the law read at the gate in Lent 806.
unlocks.gives: The grain caps of 806 and the cloak caps of 808 are shown on the market panel in every Frankish port, with a word on whether today's price is over them

unlocks.what: The ferryman's marks for the Waal
unlocks.how: Win Eilward's trust: name him to the clerk, or bring him the wood for a second punt.
unlocks.gives: No pilot is needed on the Waal between the river mouths and the parting of the streams; he tells what passed in the night

unlocks.what: A hearing for the emperor's own letter of protection
unlocks.how: From 814 to 840, with a count or bishop to speak for you, a gift to the chamber and a house the delta trusts: ask for an audience at the palace in May. In the years the emperor Louis is here himself (noviomagus.louis), a true account of a raid counts as the gift.
unlocks.gives: Opens story/unlocks_793.json unlock_title_palace_merchant (240 d): free of toll in the Frankish realm but for the tenth at Dorestad and Quentovic

unlocks.what: The word of a count's house
unlocks.how: In the winter of 880-881, carry Evesa's ransom through the rampart and bring Eberhard out.
unlocks.gives: A friend that passes to the heir; lodging and a hearing in the halls of Meginhard's kin on the IJssel and the lower Rhine

unlocks.what: Sanctuary and a name said at the altar
unlocks.how: Keep the poor's table in Lent, or hang the bell.
unlocks.gives: The church by the palace shelters you and your crew from seizure; your dead are remembered here each year (act:remember costs nothing)
